lesson.title: -er/-ste Sentence Gym
lesson.subtitle: Twenty comparison sentences with als and wie using taught adjectives

hook.title: The Comparison Gym
hook.content: Two words run all comparisons: als (than) and wie (as). Older than → älter als. As old as → so alt wie. The adjectives are your old kit: groß/klein (big/small — klein hinted), kalt/warm, gut/besser, alt/jung, hoch/niedrig? — keep hoch. Twenty reps: comparative + als, equality with so...wie, superlative with am -sten. The gym's secret: German comparisons are WORD-FOR-WORD English minus the -th/-er spelling habits — 'bigger than' = größer als, with the umlaut doing English's silent vowel change.

footnotes.title: als vs wie: One Ancestor
footnotes.content: als and wie both descend from comparative particles Germanic used interchangeably ('all as' → als, 'how/like' → wie). English split the jobs into than/as/like; German kept two: als for inequality, wie for equality. Medieval German texts mix them freely — the modern split is a tidy-up.

pattern.title: The Reps
pattern.content: Inequality: Der Kaffee ist besser als der Tee. Ich bin älter als du. Die Straße ist länger als der Garten? — länger (lang → long, hint!). Winter ist kälter als Sommer? — Sommer hint. Equality: Er ist so groß wie sein Haus? — playfully: so groß wie ein Haus. Der Zug ist so schnell wie das Auto. Superlatives: Der Mont Blanc ist am höchsten. Das Wasser ist am kältesten. Der Rhein? hint — am schönsten. Also the predicate pattern: Die beste Zeit ist heute (the best time is today — bester/beste/bestes decline like ein!).
pattern.linguist_note: Comparative adjectives before nouns decline like ein-words: ein besserer Kaffee, die beste Zeit, ein höheres Haus. The ending is the article's job-share — the adjective steps in when there is no article to carry the flag.

exercises.prompt: Inequality: 'Der Winter ist kälter _____ der Sommer.'
exercises.meaning: Der Winter ist kälter als der Sommer
exercises.explanation: Inequality takes als. wie is equality's word (so kalt wie). spät is the night-owl: später als — later than everything.

exercises.prompt: Equality: 'Der Zug ist _____ schnell wie das Auto.'
exercises.meaning: Der Zug ist so schnell wie das Auto
exercises.explanation: so...wie frames equality — 'as fast as'. als would declare the train faster. Compare times the same way: die Stunde is the yardstick.

exercises.prompt: Match the comparison sentences with their English meanings:

matching_pairs.english: The house is as big as a castle
matching_pairs.german: Das Haus ist so groß wie ein Schloss

matching_pairs.english: The test is harder than the game
matching_pairs.german: Der Test ist schwerer als das Spiel

exercises.target_answer: Ich bin älter als du, Das Wasser ist zu kalt, Kaffee ist besser als Tee, Das Haus ist so groß wie ein Schloss, Der Test ist schwerer als das Spiel
exercises.meaning: four comparison patterns and a heavyweight
exercises.explanation: als compares down the ladder, wie holds it level, zu cranks it — three tools, one gym. schwer (heavy, difficult) weighs in: schwerer als — heavier than.

exercises.prompt: Superlative it: 'hoch' → 'Der Mont Blanc ist am _____.' (the highest):
exercises.explanation: hoch → höher → am höchsten — the gh→ch word with pure umlaut all the way up.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the German sentence for 'Today is the best day':
exercises.meaning: Heute ist der beste Tag = Today is the best day
exercises.explanation: am besten is the adverb superlative; before a noun it declines: der beste Tag — the ein-family endings again.

summary.outcome: Build als/wie comparisons and am -sten superlatives with declining adjectives.
summary.takeaway: als = than, so...wie = as...as, am -sten = superlative — and before nouns the adjective declines like ein.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: adjective endings — the article's echo: der kalte Tag vs ein kalter Tag.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — build in German: "Today that is very good"
twist.explanation: Building "Heute ist das sehr gut" from the lesson's core pattern locks in -er/-ste Sentence Gym.

alt.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *aldaz — the twin of old; the l stayed, the vowel and final d/t report the shift. [wiktionary]

hoch.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hauhaz — the twin of high, with high's gh still sounding as the Ach-Laut ch. Comparative: höher (high→higher). [wiktionary]

groß.etymology_derivation: T → S/ß shift from Germanic "great". Preserved in English "gross income", "gross national product", and "a gross error" (large, not disgusting).

klein.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *klainiz 'clean, fine' — the TRUE twin of English clean; the meaning drifted from 'clean' to 'small'. [wiktionary]

als.etymology_derivation: Kin to English else (both from the *alja- 'other' family) — the comparative particle. [wiktionary]

wie.context_translation: How are you? (How goes it to you?)
wie.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *hwē, a fossilized instrumental of who/what — the same variant that gave English why. [wiktionary]

schnell.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German snel, Proto-Germanic *snellaz, meaning quick and bold; the exact English cognate is the rare word snell, still heard in northern England and Scotland. [wiktionary]

schwer.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *swēraz 'heavy, grave'; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

spät.context_phrase: Es ist schon spät in der Nacht.
spät.context_translation: It is already late at night.
spät.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *spādī; only Dutch/Low German cognates — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

spiel.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *spil 'dance'; no English cognate — English spiel is borrowed FROM German. [wiktionary]

stunde.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *stundu — cognate with archaic English stound 'hour'. [wiktionary]

humor.context_phrase: Er hat einen guten Sinn für Humor.
humor.context_translation: He has a good sense of humor.
humor.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Latin humor; the modern funny sense was a semantic loan from English humour — the same word, with English even lending it its meaning. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
